items.title: Dominic James "Nick" La Rocca Interview, 1959-10-26
items.q: In fact, I never knew Joe Oliver. I never met him.

ctx.x: What did you think about it?

I thought it was all right, but Whiteman never played no jazz. He'd taken all the arrangements from the Dixieland Jazz Band. It don't take you long to hear that. Go listen to his wang wang blues. Or any tunes that Bussie played. Bussie made this little lick that Joe Oliver made before Joe Oliver put it on the record. Da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da. Joe, if you don't believe it, listen to Hot Lips Bussie playing on Hot Lips.
That's his favorite piece. I've heard him many times. All right. The dance touch.

items.title: Dominic James "Nick" La Rocca Interview, 1958-06-09
items.q: After this time came King Oliver, Punk, and Freddie Capron... and the original Creole Band. They were the last word and swing cornet players.

ctx.x: It is an original Negro tune, which was made up down south. It was named Tiger Rag when the Dixieland Band brought it up north. Buddy, you want me to continue with this? Yeah, go on. Buddy Bolden was the hottest cornetist in the world, and he played so much that he is in the insane asylum now if he is still living. After this time came King Oliver, Punk, and Freddie Capron, that's spelled K-E-P-P-E-R-T, and the original Creole Band. They were the last word and swing cornet players. The swing pianists were Albert…

We used to have swing sessions every morning around 3 o'clock after the boys got through with their work and each man would do his bit. Quote, the first hot band to leave from the South and introduce swing music was the Creole Jazz Band, unquote, says Mr. Williams. Quote, following the Dixieland Jazz Band, which recorded Livery Stable Blues and Tiger Ray, which swept the country. The Creole Band was colored and the Dixieland Band was white and they used to play across the street from each other and used to sit in…

items.title: Dominic James "Nick" La Rocca Interview, 1958-06-09
items.q: No, I never... I don't know who this man is, but this is before my time.

ctx.x: No, I never... I don't know who this man is, but this is before my time.

Well, Bunk Johnson was supposed to be an old-time man who taught... Well, Joe Oliver. Joe Oliver in turn taught... Larry Armstrong. And that's how it goes. Nobody else played music but the syndicates, the Negroes. Nobody played music in New Orleans. As far as I know about music, and if you want the truth about it, the Negroes did not play any kind of music equal to white men at any time. Even the poorest band of white men played better than the Negroes in my days. With the exception of like Piron and...

items.title: Dominic James "Nick" La Rocca Interview, 1958-06-02
items.q: Now they say these Negroes didn't hear these records. Joe heard them. If this man heard them, Joe Oliver heard them. Because Joe, in his thing, that's what he bases his rhythm on.

ctx.x: I have a record of Virginia Blues by the Louisiana Five in which they play the third strain of Skeleton Jangle as a part of the tune. It's signed, uh, Sincerely Yours, Don Fowler. Is there anything else you want to read?

You know, that's all. Not only the Louisiana Five, but everybody. It was a field lead from the all steel music and different things out the original Dixieland jazz band. Now they say these Negroes didn't hear these records. Joe heard them. If this man heard them, Joe Oliver heard them. Because Joe, in his thing, that's what he bases his rhythm on. Because he didn't know no better. He was just a Negro that didn't know no better. Like these even white crumbs who's supposed to be historians around New Orleans. They…

The letter here from... Let me see. I'll give you the full letterhead. It's a letter from Marshall W. Stearns. Yale Hot Club, 6th Linwood Place, New Haven, Connecticut. M. W. Stearns, President. Charter Unit of the UHCA. January the 11th, 1937, Mr. D.J. La Rocca, Earl Theater, Washington, D.C. Dear Nick, I have all your records from Liberty Stable Blues to the recent disc.
